notes.meaning: Joab received word that David was weeping and mourning over the death of his son Absalom. Instead of leading a celebration for the victory that saved his kingdom, the king was completely crushed by sorrow. David was acting like a grieving father rather than a thankful ruler.

The joy of winning the battle suddenly disappeared and turned into sadness for the entire army. The soldiers heard that their king was deeply distressed over his son instead of pleased with their victory. His heavy grief made the people feel as though they had done something wrong.

The troops did not march back into the city with songs and banners of triumph. Instead, they slipped quietly into the city in shame, just like defeated soldiers sneaking away from a lost battle. They feared the king would look on them with anger for killing his son.

David covered his face in the usual manner of deep mourning and kept crying out loudly for Absalom. He repeated his son's name over and over in uncontrolled grief. His heart broke because his rebellious child had died in his sins without repentance.

Joab went directly into the house to confront the king face-to-face. He told David that his weeping brought public shame on the loyal servants who had just risked their lives to protect him, his wives, and his children. Joab spoke bluntly to force David to see how ungrateful he appeared.

Joab charged David with acting as if he loved those who hated him and hated those who loved him. By ignoring his army, David gave the impression that his generals and soldiers meant nothing to him. Joab even declared that David seemed happier if Absalom had lived and his whole loyal army had died.

Joab ordered the king to get up immediately and go speak warmly and gratefully to his troops. He swore an oath that if David refused, every soldier would desert him before morning. That loss would bring worse trouble on David than anything he had faced since his youth.

David listened to the harsh warning, mastered his feelings, and took his seat at the city gate. This gate was the public place where rulers met their people and gave judgments. When the loyal troops heard he was there, they gathered before him, while the rebels who had supported Absalom scattered to their homes.

Across the northern tribes of Israel, the people began arguing with one another about what to do next. They reminded each other that David had delivered them from the Philistines and many other enemies in the past. Even though David had been driven out by Absalom, they recognized how much they still owed him.

The people admitted that Absalom, the leader they had chosen to follow, was now dead on the battlefield. With the rebellion collapsed, they questioned why no one was stepping forward to bring David back to the throne. They were eager to restore the true king after their mistake.

Word reached David that the northern tribes were talking about bringing him back, but his own tribe of Judah remained silent. David sent the priests Zadok and Abiathar to ask the leaders of Judah why they were holding back. Since the revolt had started in Judah, the people there were likely afraid David would punish them.

David urged the priests to remind the leaders of Judah that they were his brothers and his own flesh and blood. He wanted them to know he still loved them and would not take revenge. Because of this family bond, they should have been the first, not the last, to welcome him home.

David also sent a special message to Amasa, who had led Absalom's rebel army. David appealed to their family relation and swore an oath to make Amasa the head of his forces instead of Joab. This move offered full forgiveness to the rebels and showed David's anger at Joab for killing Absalom.

This kind message and offer of pardon completely won over the people of Judah. They united in purpose as if they shared a single heart. Together they sent word asking David and all his followers to return to his palace.

David began his journey back toward Jerusalem and arrived at the Jordan River. The leaders of Judah came out to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across the water. David chose to wait for an invitation rather than force his way back into power.

Shimei rushed down with the men of Judah to meet King David at the river. Earlier, when David was fleeing Jerusalem, Shimei had cursed him and thrown stones at him. Now that David was returning in power, Shimei hurried to make peace before it was too late.

Shimei brought a thousand men from the tribe of Benjamin to demonstrate his local influence and support for the king. Saul's former servant Ziba also hurried to the river with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. Ziba was eager to please the king before his own deceit against Mephibosheth could be discovered.

A ferry boat crossed back and forth to carry the king's family and household goods safely over the river. As David was preparing to cross, Shimei fell down on the ground before him in humble submission. He showed open honor to the ruler he had once insulted.

Shimei openly begged the king not to hold his past guilt against him or remember the evil things he had done. He asked David to overlook the hateful words spoken on the day the king fled Jerusalem. He placed himself entirely at the king's mercy.

Shimei confessed that he had sinned and pointed out that he was the very first person from the northern tribes to greet the king. The term house of Joseph referred to the tribes outside Judah. By arriving first, Shimei hoped his early loyalty would win David's favor.

Abishai interrupted and argued that Shimei deserved to die for cursing the Lord's chosen king. Abishai had wanted to strike Shimei down earlier and believed the law demanded justice. He saw Shimei's past curses as treason against God's appointed ruler.

David sharply corrected Abishai and his brother for acting like adversaries trying to lead him into harshness. The king declared that no one would be put to death on the very day God had restored him to the throne of Israel. Knowing the Lord had shown him mercy, David chose forgiveness over revenge.
